utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. And good afternoon, Witness. Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examinations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this witness calls for no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Stojanovic? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would like to take the opportunity and ask several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to clarify some things that arose from your testimony yesterday. I don't think that my cross-examination will last long. We know where you worked. We know where you were, and we know that you were a member of the engineering company. Yesterday when you gave your testimony, at one point when you were talking about the 13th July, 1995, before you left for Snagovo, I shall remind you of the following. You said, I received information. I don't know whether this was something that Jokic ordered Jevtic to take my equipment and to go Snagovo. Do you remember that you said that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now clarify one thing for us. Who was it, Mr. Mitrovic, who told you to go to Snagovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jevtic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not mistaken when I say that Dragan Jevtic was the commander of the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask that before the Trial Chamber because we all know these names but we have to just state them for the record. At that moment on the 13th, in the afternoon, did you see Dragan Jokic at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was in the barracks, that he did come to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the fact that you think that he was in the barracks, did you then arrive at the conclusion that he gave this order to Jevtic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that Dragan Jokic, as the chief of engineering company, could not send you -- so many of you to Snagovo without the knowledge of his superior command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "I don't think he could," what do you mean? Are you saying that he only conveyed this order from the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, this was a major combat operation, this was the decision of the brigade command, if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The task of the chief of engineers was to convey this order to the platoon commander, and then this platoon commander conveyed that order to you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me finish with that. Dragan Jokic, as the chief of engineers, could not have issued any such order independently, without the knowledge of the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. And now let's go back to the 16th when Dragan Jokic's name was mentioned again. You said that on the 16th of July, between 8.00 and 9.00, you saw Jokic in the engineering company. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you help us with something. Am I right in saying that every morning in the brigade command, that is, in Standard, there were meetings held by the brigade staff. That is when all the tasks were distributed. Am I right in saying that? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not doing anything about clarifying the time. As a rule, there were morning briefings at the brigade command, and that's when tasks were given to battalion commanders, staff officers, and they were told what they were supposed to do. This makes sense to me. I would like to know whether this conversation between you and Dragan Jokic, which took place between 8.00 and 9.00, according to you, was before such a meeting or after such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it in a different way. As a matter of principle, orders given to the engineering company, were they, as a rule, conveyed after tasks were distributed in the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that day, on that morning, on the 16th, did you discuss a need to engage the engineering company for asanacija, or were you just given the task to go to Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just told by Jokic to go to Kozluk and I was also told that Lazarevic would be waiting there for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said, and I would like you to confirm that today, Jokic didn't tell you what you were supposed to do in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Once you left for Kozluk with the Skip, you didn't know what your task would be, what you were supposed to do there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the interview that you gave on the 15th of March, 2002, this issue was discussed, but just for the record let's clarify some things. When Major Jokic gave you this order, did you notice anything unusual in his behaviour or in his actions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You're saying that you left for Kozluk and that by the Vitinka company you met with Damjan Lazarevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And Damjan Lazarevic instructed you as to what you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You saw the hole. Am I right in saying that these were gravel holes, that is, the gravel that had been excavated?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So these holes had already been excavated, and this is where the victims' bodies were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not your task to dig any new holes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Lazarevic told you that your task was to bury the bodies in the already existing holes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, let's try and explain to the Trial Chamber where this all is. Am I right in saying that this location, these holes, were by the public road leading from Kozluk towards the Drina river and on towards the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, on to the ferry on the Drina river?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were the holes by that road?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that this is not a secret place. Those holes were very close to the road?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. This is not a secret place. The holes were by the road, by the public road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Help us, please, with the following: When I say that there was a ferry on the Drina river leading towards the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, what kind of a place is that? What kind of a ferry crossing is that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the Drina river, was there an embankment? Was there a place from which you cross the river towards the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when you were saying that you only worked about half an hour with this machine, that is, the Skip Torpedo, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your machine, let me put it that way, your machine could not do the job for which you were sent, because it was very weak, according to you. It did not have enough power and not enough capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the machine was not in order. It was working with only 30 per cent of its normal capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said that the machine was weak, that it did not have enough capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a construction machine that was used for digging canals and for minor works, road works, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show us with your hands how wide the claws are.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The width of that claw was 1 metre, 80 centimetres. That is the front claw. And the back claw, in the back, was about 60 centimetres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that these claws were not adjusted for easy burial; they were adjusted for excavation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front one was for loading, and the back one was for the digging of canals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well yesterday, the burial of the victims which were in two or three holes, according to you, was carried out by the ULT-220 that arrived subsequently. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I think you and the counsel are speaking the same language, so please make a pause after hearing the question put to you by the counsel. Do you understand that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So since we speak the same language, on your screen where once you see that the text stops, you can start answering your question. That will make our interpreters' life easier. Mr. Mitrovic, on the 16th, after your meeting with Dragan Jokic in the morning hours, did you see him again in Kozluk, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him, either in Kozluk or anywhere else. I didn't see him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So I would be right in saying that he didn't arrive in Kozluk while this job lasted. He didn't supervise your work. He didn't control what you were doing there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not arrive in Kozluk at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And yesterday you said that once you returned to the base, you didn't see him, you didn't report to him as to what you had done and what you hadn't done. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, and I didn't see him, I didn't report to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that Lazarevic was the one who told you what to do, Lazarevic was the one who let you go upon the work was completed, and Lazarevic is the commander of the road platoon. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You are a member of the road platoon of the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your immediate superior is Damjan Lazarevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was my platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To Ms. Davis' question, you said yesterday that when the company commander was absent, Damjan Lazarevic was subordinate to Dragan Jokic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? What did you mean when you say subordinate to? Or maybe I should break this question in two. Am I right in saying that the company commander is the one who commands the company?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that during these days, that is, on the 14th and the 15th, in the command of the engineering company, there was also Slavko Bogicevic, whom you refer to as a moralist?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know he was there on the 14th. I don't remember whether he was there on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, according to the principle of unity of command, to whom is the company of a platoon subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Am I right in saying, because we have had testimony to this effect, that a company commander is subordinate to the chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. You don't have a military education, so it's quite clear to me that you cannot speak about the rules regulating that issue; however, I was leading up to the following question. Let me just find the word you used. He was subordinated you said. What did this mean when you said it? What did you mean by it when the company commander is absent?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the company commander is absent, then he transmitted our orders to us and told us what we were to do; that's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. So he is not the one who actually gives the orders, but he only transmits the orders because the company commander is temporarily absent?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will finish with one final question. Could you please help us to clarify what you mean when you say a moralist in a company, or rather, what was Slavko Bogicevic's duties in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes he was on duty in the barracks, sometimes he stood in for the company commander, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So Slavko Bogicevic was the one who stood in for the company commander when he was absent?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Yesterday some documents were shown to you and you spoke very convincingly about them. I only wanted to confirm my understanding of what follows from your testimony. The document giving you instructions to use the Skip Torpedo was shown to you, your work order, that is. And according to this document, on the 14th of July, the Skip was in Orahovac. You remember that. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 14th, when you left Orahovac in the afternoon -- or rather, when you went to the base from Snagovo, you did not go to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me just finish this topic, the machine, the Torpedo, did it go to Orahovac? Did somebody else drive it to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It didn't go to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you explained to us that this was probably drawn up in order to justify the fuel used. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The other document that was shown to you was the travel order for the backhoe excavator, and you replied that this backhoe excavator was a machine, which on that day, the 14th, or rather, the 15th of July, was not used because it had broken down. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information that the machine BGH-700, the backhoe excavator and Cvijetin Ristanovic testified to this that on the 14th and 15th, it went to Orahovac. Am I right in saying that he was not referring to the same machine, that there were two backhoe excavators, one of which did go to Orahovac, and the other one didn't go but remained in the command because the machine had broken down?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there when the backhoe excavator left for Orahovac. I wasn't in the unit at the time, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the excavator that had broken down, where was it on the 14th and the 15th? Where was it parked, so to say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Josanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Josanica," you're referring to the village of Josanica where there is a quarry?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So that if the travel order for this excavator says that it worked in Orahovac or in Petkovci, according to you this is not correct because the machine had broken down and it was actually in Josanica. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, would you help me clarify the situation with regard to the machines. Can you remember how many machines there were in good working order in the engineering unit at the time. Is it true that there was the Skip Torpedo and the BGH-700?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the Torpedo, but as for the BGH-700, I don't know whether it was in the engineers' unit at the time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you help us by saying how many engineers' members there were who were able to drive these machines on the 14th and 15th, apart from you, Miladinovic, and Ristanovic. Was anyone else there in the unit who was able to drive those machines?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that all the other construction machines were mobilised according to need from the brigade command when there was a job to be done. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now to go back to the 15th of July, which according to us was a Saturday, and you testified that on that day you were in the command of the engineers' company and that you did not have any specific tasks to perform. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that as far as you can remember, on that day, apart from you, Vojislav Sekanic was in the engineers' unit and a guard. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you all this for the following reason: Mr. Mitrovic, did you see or hear anyone - I don't know who - from the engineers' company who on that morning or on that day, the 15th of July, could have taken a machine, any machine, and go to Petkovci to the dam there and work on burials?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no machine there that someone could take.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So I'm right in saying that on the 15th, there were neither machines nor machine operators in the unit who could have gone to Petkovci and work on the burials?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no other machine operator, apart from me in the unit. There was only myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After this, that is, after the 15th of July, did you hear from any of your colleagues from the engineers' company that they had been at Petkovci and worked on burials on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't hear anyone say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. I just wanted to put one other question to you. As a rule, what does the morning look like in the engineers' company? Am I right that you line up, that your duties are assigned to you, as is usual?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that when you're lined up, the flag is raised, your commands are read out to you. This is done by the company commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether on the 15th in the morning, this was the procedure that was followed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why, because there were no soldiers around; is that the reason?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ristanovic told us the same thing. I just wanted to check this. If I'm correct, 15 of you, according to the order that arrived from the brigade that Dragan transmitted, were to go to Snagovo and be on the frontline. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the engineers' company, Dragan Jokic, or Jevtic was with you all this time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, I would now like to go back to the 16th and to the ULT-220. You said that this machine did not belong to the engineers' company, that it was owned by the quarry. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Rade Boskovic came to Kozluk with this machine. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you assist me with this. Do you remember whether Rade Boskovic on that day was wearing civilian clothes or a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I think he was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We have lists here of the members of the engineers' company, and that's why I want to ask you the following: Am I right in saying that Rade Boskovic at that time, that is, mid-July, was not a member of the engineers' company and that he had a work obligation in the quarry?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he -- yes, I think he had a work obligation in the quarry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this could be the reason why he arrived in civilian clothes, rather than a military uniform. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the call-up of military conscripts, such as Rade Boskovic, Vojislav Sekanic, or anybody else was carried out by the brigade command through the Ministry of Defence and this could not be done just by someone going and saying, I'm mobilising the soldier or this employee, this worker?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the procedure is, but I think it goes through the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. When you say it goes through the brigade command, you're referring both to soldiers and to equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that there was a certain procedure to be followed, that's at least what we know, that someone could not walk into a company and say: I'm taking this machine because I need it for the army, for the military. There has to be a procedure that's followed. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I just wanted to put a few questions to you with respect to the reburials, the count in the indictment that refers to the reburials. Did you hear that in the period of August and October 1995, there were reburials of these, as we call them, primary grave sites or burial sites?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that you spoke of this in your interview, but we didn't hear about this yesterday. So I just wanted you to assist us by telling us where you were in this period, August, September, and October 1995. What were you doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now what we did or where.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of you in that period ask to go and work on the reburials?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, did you hear any one of the members of the engineers' company, your colleagues, or any equipment take part in this activity of reburial?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that as far as you know personally, you personally did not take part in any activity connected with reburials?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. And one last question. Since when have you known Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1992, when he came to my house to see about the machine, to have me go to the engineers' unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of 1992, yesterday I understood you to say that at the beginning of the wartime events, you were a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in 1992 when a sabotage group or an infiltrated group in the area of Klisa took part in fighting in which there were casualties on both the Serb and Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I believe the witness testified very briefly about this yesterday, but I'm not sure what the relevance is for further questioning on this. It's not relevant to the case and the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. What's the relevance of this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall bring it to an end with a question about the character of Dragan Jokic and the activities that he had in the burial of the bodies that had been left behind after this operation. So this is the relevance of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may try.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, let's bring this to an end. You said that you were aware of the fact that there were victims on both sides. Are you aware of the fact that at that time Captain Jokic was in charge of the action of pulling out the bodies of the fallen Bosniaks and that in accordance with the Geneva Conventions he carried out the handover of the bodies in -- to the commander of the other side, Mr. Semso Omerovic [phoen]. And that was done through an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said you've known Dragan since 1992. What can you tell us about him? What kind of a person he is, what kind of an officer he was.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, he was an a good man. We cooperated well. He was not a bad man at all at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your contacts with him, did you notice or feel any nationalism, religious or ethnic intolerance, or things like that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this was my last question. I have no further questions and I would like to thank you, Your Honours, and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any redirect? Ms. Davis?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Witness, you were just asked a few moments ago about Mr. Jokic's involvement in the burial of -- or in the pulling out bodies of fallen Bosniaks in 1992 and you were asked whether the Geneva Convention was followed in that process. Can I ask you, in your instructions from Mr. Lazarevic regarding covering up the bodies at Kozluk, whether anyone present there checked the bodies there to see if anyone was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was checked, but I believe that nobody was alive because there was already the smell of bodies and I don't think that there was anybody alive out there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And in your presence, nobody checked the bodies to see if anyone was alive?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: In your presence, did anyone check the bodies for identification papers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not while I was there, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: In your presence, were any bodies put into body bags?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: In your presence, was there any effort to register the victims?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, were the bodies that you were involved in covering up at Kozluk ever turned over to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or to any Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, are there any documents to tender? Ms. Davis?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, all of the documents that we have shown to this witness have been previously admitted into evidence, so we don't have anything to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no documents to tender at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of this courtroom. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, there is a housekeeping matter to deal with. That is, last week we asked the parties, especially the Defence counsel, to raise any objections to the admission of Mr. Butler's evidence -- I mean that evidence introduced through Mr. Butler's testimony. The deadline was this Monday, and up until now we have received no objections except some intercepts raised by Ms. Sinatra orally last week. So we believe that this Bench is in the position to make a decision that that evidence introduced through Mr. Butler's testimony will be admitted into the evidence, except the intercepts. And we reserve the right to deal with it at a later stage. It is so decided. Well, maybe somebody from the Prosecution team could brief us about the next witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. This will be a witness who has only one protective measure, that I think like the previous ones, image distortion. But just for the sake of caution, I would like to ask him, again in your presence, whether he's fine that his name be identified to the public. He said he's fine with it, but I think it's easier, it's better, if I do this in your presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Have you explained to this witness about the protective measures? We find it very strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we did it, Mr. President. And he just says he does not want that people on TV or in the public gallery see his face. But he says, my name is fine, I want to testify under my full name. That's what he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember that we met yesterday in my office, in fact, on the previous day as well, and you were advised of your right to remain silent and to have a lawyer present. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you waived these rights, and we discussed your evidence without the presence of a lawyer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also told us that you would be willing to testify today in this courtroom under these conditions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you're ready to proceed and answer questions without the presence of a lawyer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you also told me that you wanted your image to be distorted, but that you're fine that your name be known to the public. Can you confirm that today.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: All right. Let me then start with a few personal details. Can you state for the record your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Marko Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Majo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 30th March, 1964, in Lupoglavo village, Kladanj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you briefly tell us your education. Do you have a university degree?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the university of Tuzla. I majored in the protection at work. So I'm an engineer of protection at work and in environmental protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what's your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you have a job?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what would that be?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the electrical distribution as an anti-fire protection officer and an officer for protection at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what are you doing currently?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm now testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. Sorry for my stupid question. What's your current occupation? Work-related, your current occupation, work-related?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am an officer for the protection at work and anti-fire protection at the company called electrical distribution in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Let me briefly ask you about your military career. I understand you had some education, some training, with the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I served in the army in 1983, that was my compulsory military obligation, and I was in the army for 12 months in Sarajevo. That was the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a rank when you left?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I left, I was a lance corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we will later talk about 1995, but let me just ask you briefly about the prior years. In 1993 or 1994, did you have a brief assignment as an assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For some six or seven months in the 1st Battalion that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that would be the 1st Battalion of which brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let me turn to 1995. Were you in the army as well in that year?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In March -- from March to March, I had a work obligation in the company Glinica Birac in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in terms of army, did you have a function in the army in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was, again, mobilised in 1995 in March, and I was assistant commander of the 6th Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. That was my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who appointed you to this position?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us who that was.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, as a deputy brigade commander, who was your commander -- sorry, deputy battalion commander, who was your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My commander was Captain Ostoja Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what your duties were as a deputy battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My duty as a deputy battalion commander was see to the communications in the battalion; that means I was in charge of the communication with the units on the frontline and the command of the brigade. And I also assisted the battalion commander with other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, who would be in command of the battalion in the absence of your commander, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the absence of the battalion commander, it would be the deputy commander, and that is only in the absence of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that would be yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there long absences of your battalion commander while you were his deputy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. Only if he went home to rest for a day if the situation in the Zvornik Brigade was calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to show the Judges or explain to the Judges a few of the locations in that area where you were stationed. If you, please, could be shown an exhibit that's a map of Eastern Bosnia with battalion positions. And I don't think it has a number yet. Yes, it's been assigned exhibit P668. Now, if you could take a moment for yourself and just look at the map, and then my first question would be if you could show us the city of Zvornik. Perhaps if the map could be moved up a little bit, the other way around. Yes, thanks. To the city of Zvornik again.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You are pointing to the bottom of the map in the middle?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you tell us where the positions of your battalion were, and if you could start with the command post, please.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The command post of the 6th Battalion was in Petkovci, in the old school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you have -- do you recognise who did the markings on this map?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you just mentioned where the command post was, and I believe you had indicated that spot where there is an A. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, letter A. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you mentioned that it's in Petkovci, and you said it's the old school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us where the forward command post was, if you had any of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The forward command post was in a different part marked by letter B.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us roughly the distance between those two command posts.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some 2 and a half to 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many companies did your battalion have at that time in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were four infantry companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us how they were allocated in your area.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The first company was deployed on the right flank, and it bordered on the Sapna river. And then the second company is up here. The third company and the fourth company are next to the Bajkovac river.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I see a yellow line. Do you know what that yellow line indicates?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The yellow line indicates the area of our defence, the defence of the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks. And you just indicated the location of those companies, and I believe you started with the first company on the right side, and then went on to the second and third company. And the fourth company would be on the left side of your defence line?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us who your neighbours were, and I'm asking about battalions.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Our right-hand side neighbour was, I believe, the 3rd Battalion, yes. And on the left-hand side on the left flank, there was the 4th Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. I have a couple more questions about the backdrop of these events. How many members -- how many soldiers did this 6th Battalion have in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the exact number, but there were some 400 troops, together with the reserve battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So when you say "reserve battalion," you had four normal battalions and one reserve battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain what you meant by reserve battalion.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said that the battalion had 400 troops, together with the command and the rear of the battalion, not the reserve, the rear of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, July 1995, where did you spend your time when you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the command of the 6th Battalion in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you were assigned to be in charge of communications. Can you briefly tell us what means of communication you had available in your battalion and up to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We had the three systems of communications in the battalion. We had the civilian connection, then we had a wire communication, and a radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did these communication means work, or were there times when you couldn't communicate with each other or up to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They mostly worked. Only sometimes where it happened that there was no communication, but one of these means of communication were always functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you about an incident in 1993 or 1994 when a Muslim was taken prisoner. Can you explain to us what happened, who was involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This happened in 1993 or 1994, I don't know exactly when, but it was springtime. A Muslim, a member of a Muslim unit, strayed amongst our soldiers. He was drunk, and he was taken by our soldiers on the line. Then they brought him to the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did you do with him at the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We called the military police to the brigade to take him over and to take him to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you question him at the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We asked him a few things, but most of the questioning took place in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was that the procedure that you had implemented to deal with Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me take you to July 1995. How were you made aware that the enclave of Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we heard about it on the radio that Vlasenica [as interpreted] had fallen. It was on the news on the radio, and probably people from the brigade knew about it, but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did people from your battalion, let me ask you about your battalion, have troops in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We had about 90 soldiers who were active in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember who was in charge of those troops?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was a man who was my neighbour, Slavisa Marjanovic. He was the commander of the platoon that was at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this was the platoon that was formed out of your 6th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said just a minute ago in response to my question about how you were made aware that the enclave of Srebrenica fell, you said, or least that's what's written in the English version of the transcript, that, and I quote: "We heard about it on the radio that Vlasenica had fallen." Did you mean Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I meant Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I believe, Mr. President. I don't know if you want a break now. We started five minutes later, but perhaps it's easier for everybody to get ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me turn to the 14th of July. Do you remember a phone call you had received on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who called you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The duty officer from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: From which brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember at what time you received that phone call?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was between 11.00 and 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where were you when you received that phone call?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did the duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade tell you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He told me that in about two hours, Muslim prisoners would arrive from Srebrenica, and they would be accommodated in the primary school in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us before the break that your command was stationed at the primary school. Can you tell us, are there two primary schools in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We were in the old school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the prisoners would be brought to which school then?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The new school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, why did you take this phone call?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My commander, Ostoja Stanisic, took about 30 soldiers from our battalion to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, and they were to be sent to Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, which line did you get this phone call? Was it the public line? A land line? A secure line? Over radio? Can you tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was the wire communication line, an inductor wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what an inductor wire is.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's a wire connection through which we had communications with the brigade. There was an inductor in the command, and this was connected to the duty officer in the battalion. And he switched the line over to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was it possible to intercept this line of communication?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Only if the line was cut, but it was functioning at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, by intercepting, I mean was it possible for somebody else, for instance your enemy, to listen to this conversation you had with the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when you received that information, what were you thinking? What were your thoughts about these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Personally I thought they would be locked up and that after a certain period of time they would be exchanged. That was what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you talked about this school, the new school. What was its use? Did you use it? Did your battalion use it for any purpose?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From time to time, intervention platoons were put up there, they were quartered in the school, and they assisted the battalion if the battalion area was attacked or if there were indicia that the Muslims might attack the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you keep a log -- did you or somebody else keep a log of incoming phone calls from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that your commander was away in Zvornik bringing troops to the brigade. Now, did you inform him about the phone call you had?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, when he got back to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how long after the phone call was that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Two, or two and a half hours, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what happened next in relation to these prisoners? Did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They arrived -- I don't know at exactly what time, because in the afternoon I went down to the primary school -- not to the school itself, but the crossroads, because Commander Ostoja Stanisic sent me there after the duty officer from the brigade asked that we find a certain Colonel Beara, whom I did not know, and Dragan Nikolic was supposed to be with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you know why your battalion commander told you to go to find Beara? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. After talking to the duty officer from the brigade, he told me that they said we should find him and that he should report to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, that he should call them, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So are you saying there was a second phone call with the duty officer that Mr. Stanisic talked to the duty officer of the brigade? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. Stanisic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, tell me, since you also talked to the duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade, did you know at that time who the duty officer was of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I didn't know exactly, because there were officers who took turns, and I don't know which of them it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you didn't know exactly, did you make a guess at that time who it could have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. It calls for speculation. I think that if you go back to his previous question, he received the answer. Now he's asking the gentleman if he could have guessed or if he could guess, so I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think this kind of question is not proper. You should not invite the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, go to the school of the -- of Petkovci, as ordered by your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you find Beara, as you were told to do so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I found Beara at the crossroads on the main road, together with Drago Nikolic and a few military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how far away from your command headquarters was the new school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: About 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us that you met a person called Nikolic. Can you tell us who this Nikolic was.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was the assistant commander for security in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, whom did you address? Did you address Beara or did you address Nikolic when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know Beara personally, so I addressed Drago Nikolic, and he told me that this was indeed Beara. I greeted him, and then I transmitted the message to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I told him that they had called from the brigade and that he should call them back urgently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber how Beara looked. What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't be certain, but he had a camouflage uniform. He was about 60 years old with grey hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he respond anything?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you described to us what you saw when you arrived at that crossroad, a few military policemen you told us. Do you know from which military brigade they were?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know them personally. I don't know what brigade they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you see -- when you were at that crossroad, did you see the new school as well where the prisoners were supposed to be held?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How far away was it from where you were standing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some 60 or 70 metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whether the prisoners had arrived at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I saw the troops who were providing security for the school, so I suppose that the prisoners had already been there, in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And by "troops," what do you mean? Are these the military policemen you had described earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms, different uniforms. I didn't know any of them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And by "different," do you mean different from the policemen you have described?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some wore camouflage uniforms, some wore olive-drab uniforms, like the former JNA used to wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you know from which unit they were?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see any vehicles in that area, around the school and the crossroad?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the road, there were a few trucks and a few buses that drove the Muslims. I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what did you do next? Did you return to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I returned to the battalion command immediately, immediately after having conveyed the message to Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did you do there at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I informed Commander Stanisic that I had conveyed the message and that Colonel Beara was now aware of the fact that he was to call back the command of the Zvornik Brigade immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what your commander, Mr. Stanisic, did after you told him that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He let the brigade know that the colonel had been informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whom in the brigade he called?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was probably the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what were you doing that evening? We are still on the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you hear any gunfire that evening?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Late in the afternoon, there were gun shots from the direction of the school; that's what we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, since that was only 5, 600 metres away from your command post, did you or your commander or anybody else do something in relation to these gunfires?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since the commander was there, I was not duty-bound to do anything. And I don't remember that the commander did anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Weren't you worried, hearing gunfire so close to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you discuss the gunfire or, indeed, the prisoner issue with your commander, any, in that evening?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We probably did, but I don't remember the conversation that took place in the battalion command. We discussed quite a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next day, 15th [Realtime transcript read in error "16th"] of July, 1995. Just briefly, what were you doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Early in the morning, I went, together with a few soldiers, to the 4th Company. I was sent there by the commander to see what was going on there, because we had been informed from the line that two of our trenches had been destroyed by the Muslim forces, either by mortar fire or a hand-held mortar, I don't know exactly. In any case, they had been destroyed and the troops had withdrawn from these trenches. I went up there to inspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, may I interrupt you for a moment. I'm looking at the transcript and it says on line 19, page 36, we are still on the 14th. And then next page, line 12: "Let me turn to the next day, 16th of July." Can you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much for your observation and attention, Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, you just described what you were doing on the certain day. Which date are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of July, in the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And thank you very much, Witness, for that clarification. Where did you spend the evening of 15th July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We were in the battalion command up to 1.00 in the night. And then I, my commander, and other members of the command went to the forward command post, and I went to the 4th Company that had manned these two trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you went to the same location you have been during the previous day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why did you go there? Were you ordered to do so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Around 10.00 or 11.00 in the evening on the 15th of July, the duty officer from the brigade called and he wanted to talk to the forward command post of our battalion. He wanted somebody to go there. And in the meantime, the platoon commander from the 4th Company arrived and asked all of us to go there because the troops were scared. And we did that around 1.00 or half past 1.00 in the morning. We went to the forward command post, and I myself went to the sector of the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, where did you stay that night? I mean, where were you then the following morning?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I spent the night until the morning in the sector of the 4th Company, in the left-most flank. I was in a trench, and together with me there were two soldiers from the engineers company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have casualties?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Early in the morning, around 7.00, I believe, a shell fell into the trench where I was, killing two of our soldiers, members of the VRS. One of them was a member of the engineers' company. I don't know his name. I know his family name was Micic and that he was a native of the area around Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in the course of that day, and we are now on the 16th of July, were you yourself wounded?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded between 1.00 and 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was on the left flank of the 4th Company. I and a few other soldiers from that company waited for the military police and the sick and wounded who were being pulled out from the command of the 4th Battalion, because they had come under heavy fire of the Muslim forces from both sides. We waited for them where our Browning was, and some 10 or 15 minutes later, as we were returning to our reserve positions where the line used to be, that is what I was wounded, together with seven or our soldiers and also two or three of our soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Of what nature were your wounds?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded in my -- both lower extremities. I was wounded in both legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you get treatment?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I was wounded, my soldiers carried me down to Petkovci. I couldn't walk from there. I was transported to the Zenica hospital where I was hospitalised for seven, eight, or nine days, I don't remember exactly for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Reading the transcript it says Zenica hospital. Were you treated at the Zenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, while in the hospital, did you hear what happened to the prisoners which you were concerned with in the new Petkovci school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While I was in the hospital, some two or three days later I heard that all the prisoners who were in the school had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: People came to visit me, soldiers, my family, friends, and my commander Ostoja Stanisic also came. So I really can't remember who it was who told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know where the prisoners were executed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The story was they were killed on the red mud [Realtime transcript read in error "road"].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember how far the red dam, as you call it if I correctly understood you, how far away that dam is from the new school in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but since I lived in Lupe and Djulici, the dam could be seen from my house and I believe that it was a kilometre away from my house and some 2 kilometres away from Petkovci. I don't know exactly how far it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In the transcript it says something about a road. I believe you said they were killed by a dam. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that they were killed by the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said you were a number of days in the hospital. Did you eventually return to your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some ten days later, I was discharged. And after that, I received shots and I had to go back to the hospital for my wounds to be dressed. So I didn't return immediately to my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When did you eventually return to the battalion? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was around the 10th of August. I can't remember exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did your battalion or the brigade ever investigate into the killings of these prisoners at the -- in the Petkovci area?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know if there was any investigation into that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you personally, apart from talking to the investigators from this Tribunal, were you ever interviewed, yourself, in relation to those events, either by the army authorities or civilian local authorities?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody ever questioned me, save for the OTP in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether anybody from the VRS or from the police or whoever was punished by military authorities or civilian authorities, local authorities, because of these events?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you hear anything about reburials, meaning that bodies were taken out of mass graves in the area you were present?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After some time, people were talking -- and I don't know who it was, whether it was the army, the civilians, the locals, I don't know who was talking. But there were stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us in more detail, if you can. I don't know what these stories were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to ask if I could please object at this time. The questions are such that: Have you heard? What were the stories going around? I think in order to keep the record clean, we have the witness here who can testify about his personal knowledge about what took place. But: Have you heard? We don't know what period of time he heard about this. Was it 1996, was it 1997? I think this is so unspecific and hearsay upon hearsay -- and we don't even know where the hearsay is coming from or the time period that he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the time period is quite clear, and this witness is clearly saying that he heard some stories about this. I don't think there is any problem. As you understand that the hearsay evidence is still admissible in this courtroom. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these stories said.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I only know that people who were killed were reburied, but I don't know where. And to be honest, I wasn't interested in knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions before we finish. Do you know Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Back in July 1995, what was his function?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was the commander of the engineers' unit company I don't know what formation it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was that part of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the company or the battalion or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just told us that he was the commander of the engineers' unit company, and I'm asking you whether this company was part of a specific brigade.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know him well, Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know him that well. We didn't have close contacts. I would see him in the brigade, but we didn't have any common points when it came to the troops, that is, his troops and my troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know Dragan Jevtic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, the interpreters couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What answer is that? Dragan Jevtic you mean? I know Dragan Jevtic.
